title: 1 Chronicles 18:9–17
context: Tou king of Hamath sends his son Hadoram with gifts, which David dedicates to the LORD with spoil from the nations. Abishai defeats Edom in the Valley of Salt, and the chapter closes with David’s just rule and a list of his officials. The account parallels 2 Samuel 8:9–18 and differs in several names and numbers, including the victor and the defeated people in the Valley of Salt, the names of a priest and the scribe, and the description of David’s sons. The notes name these differences without resolving them. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about God’s blessing on David’s reign.

verses.text: When Tou king of Hamath heard that David had struck all the army of Hadadezer king of Zobah,
verses.arminianNotes:
Tou king of Hamath hears that David has struck all the army of Hadadezer king of Zobah. News of the victory spreads.

Arminian readers see surrounding kings taking notice and having to decide how to respond to Israel’s king.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Samuel 8:9 spells the king’s name Toi. The narrative sets up an embassy of goodwill.

Reformed readers see God making David’s name great, as promised in 17:8. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the growing recognition of David’s kingdom.

verses.text: he sent Hadoram his son to King David to greet him and to bless him, because he had fought against Hadadezer and struck him (for Hadadezer had wars with Tou); and he had with him all kinds of vessels of gold and silver and bronze.
verses.arminianNotes:
Tou sends his son Hadoram to greet and bless David, with all kinds of vessels of gold, silver, and bronze, because Hadadezer had warred against Tou. Peace follows victory.

Arminian readers see friendship sought rather than conquest.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Samuel 8:10 names the son Joram. The narrative does not explain the different names.

Reformed readers see nations bringing gifts to David’s throne. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note the different names plainly without resolving them.

verses.text: King David also dedicated these to the LORD, with the silver and the gold that he carried away from all the nations: from Edom, from Moab, from the children of Ammon, from the Philistines, and from Amalek.
verses.arminianNotes:
David dedicates these gifts to the LORD, with the silver and gold carried away from Edom, Moab, Ammon, the Philistines, and Amalek. He keeps nothing back for himself.

Arminian readers see grateful devotion.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Samuel 8:12 lists Syria where Chronicles lists Edom, and adds the plunder of Hadadezer. The difference is noted, not resolved.

Reformed readers see David gathering for the house he may not build. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Moreover Abishai the son of Zeruiah struck eighteen thousand of the Edomites in the Valley of Salt.
verses.arminianNotes:
Abishai son of Zeruiah strikes eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. The victory is credited to David’s commander.

Arminian readers see God working through David’s officers as well as the king.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Samuel 8:13 says David struck eighteen thousand Syrians in the Valley of Salt; Chronicles names Abishai and the Edomites. The difference is noted plainly, without resolving it.

Reformed readers see the victory as part of God’s gift to David’s reign. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: He put garrisons in Edom; and all the Edomites became servants to David. The LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verses.arminianNotes:
David puts garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites become his servants. Again the LORD gives victory to David wherever he goes.

Arminian readers see the refrain of verse 6 crediting the whole campaign to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
The parallel in 2 Samuel 8:14 repeats the mention of garrisons throughout Edom; Chronicles states it once.

Reformed readers see all of David’s victories framed as God’s work. Both traditions read the refrain as clear shared ground.

verses.text: David reigned over all Israel; and he executed justice and righteousness for all his people.
verses.arminianNotes:
David reigns over all Israel and executes justice and righteousness for all his people. Victory abroad is matched by just rule at home.

Arminian readers see the ideal of kingship as rule for the good of the people.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse matches 2 Samuel 8:15. Justice and righteousness are later linked with the messianic king (Isaiah 9:7).

Reformed readers see David at his best pointing to Christ’s perfectly just reign. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder;
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab son of Zeruiah is over the army, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud is recorder. The list of officials begins.

Arminian readers see the people who carry out the king’s rule, including Joab, whose role in David’s story is sometimes troubling.
verses.reformedNotes:
The names match 2 Samuel 8:16. The recorder’s exact duties are not described.

Reformed readers see God’s blessing in stable government. Both traditions read this as historical background and shared ground, and neither finds a theological dispute in the list.

verses.text: Zadok the son of Ahitub and Abimelech the son of Abiathar were priests; Shavsha was scribe;
verses.arminianNotes:
Zadok son of Ahitub and Abimelech son of Abiathar are priests, and Shavsha is scribe. Worship and administration stand side by side.

Arminian readers see the place of worship in David’s kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Samuel 8:17 reads Ahimelech rather than Abimelech and names the scribe Seraiah rather than Shavsha. The differences are noted, not resolved.

Reformed readers caution against overstating what the list says. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and the sons of David were chief officials serving the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
Benaiah son of Jehoiada is over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and David’s sons are chief officials serving the king. The list closes with the royal household.

Arminian readers see David’s sons holding high positions at court.
verses.reformedNotes:
2 Samuel 8:18 calls David’s sons “chief ministers”; Chronicles says “chief officials serving the king.” The difference in wording is noted, not settled.

Reformed readers see a royal guard under Benaiah. Both traditions read this as shared ground.
